video_title: Elad Gil: Most AI Companies Should Sell Now
gist: Elad Gil argues AI has compressed a decade of progress into a year, with Anthropic and OpenAI going from zero to roughly a trillion dollars, but most AI startups are priced as if they were Anthropic, so many should seriously consider selling in the next 12-18 months, as dot-com and 2021 precedents show. He also covers recursive self-improvement (80-90% of lab code AI-generated), oligopoly market structure, AI roll-ups, slower bio/materials adoption, and founder traits.

themes.theme: AI adoption speed and diffusion lag

insights.claim: Elad Gil says two AI labs, Anthropic and OpenAI, went from essentially nothing to roughly a trillion dollars of market cap in about five years, one of the most accelerated technology adoption runs in history.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Sets the reference class that private-market investors are now (mis)using to price every AI startup.
insights.quote: over the last four or five years, we've seen two companies go from zero to a trillion dollars of market cap from nothing

insights.claim: Gil notes the leading labs are approaching around $100 billion of revenue each within five years, which he frames as real adoption rather than an overinflated price.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Supports the view that lab valuations are backed by revenue, unlike most of the startups priced off them.
insights.quote: they're also hitting like 100 billion of revenue in five years. Like think of that. That's insane. That's real adoption.

insights.claim: Gil describes a diffusion gradient: AI labs are 6-9 months ahead of the average Silicon Valley engineer via internal models, Silicon Valley engineers are 6-12 months ahead of engineers elsewhere, and ordinary users (e.g. in Paris) still use ChatGPT for basic doc cleanup.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Most of AI's economic impact has not yet diffused; adoption-driven revenue upside outside the Bay Area is still ahead.
insights.quote: the labs are say six to nine months ahead of the average engineer here because they have internal models

insights.claim: Gil argues one year of AI progress now equals roughly three to five years of a normal technology cycle, so companies rise and fall unusually fast.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Compresses holding-period assumptions; competitive positions in AI should be re-underwritten far more often.
insights.quote: every year an AI is like three to five years in a normal cycle

insights.claim: Gil points out that a year earlier an MIT report claimed 90% of AI was useless and articles argued AI ROI did not justify more investment, a view the subsequent year of progress overturned.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Consensus skepticism on AI ROI has recently been wrong; be wary of fading the trend on ROI narratives alone.

insights.claim: Gil frames the current AI moment as 'punctuated equilibrium': a burst of new companies that will typically be followed by consolidation in which only some companies and use cases survive.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Expect a shakeout; position for survivors and acquirers rather than the long tail of new entrants.

insights.claim: Gil predicts the next 12 months will bring even more AI progress than the last 12, with diffusion accelerating and first real impacts beyond language and online use cases, though full diffusion will take about a decade.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Supports continued spend and capability growth; watch for AI impact in physical-world sectors as the next leg.
insights.quote: I think we'll see potentially even more progress in the next year than we saw in the last year

insights.claim: Gil expects semiconductor design, chip firmware and kernel writing to become largely AI-driven, shortening chip design cycles and making migration onto new chipsets dramatically faster.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Faster porting to new chipsets could erode software lock-in for incumbent accelerators and speed new-chip adoption.
insights.quote: you're able to migrate onto new chipsets dramatically faster than they ever have been

themes.theme: Startup valuations and the 'sell now' case

insights.claim: Gil says AI pre-seed rounds that were about $1 million at a $10 million valuation in 2022 are now $10-20 million at $100-200 million valuations for three people with an idea, often with tranched rounds at $500 million raised simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Early-stage AI entry prices are ~10x higher than in 2022, sharply raising the bar for venture returns.
insights.quote: They're raising $10 million, $20 million at a$100 to $200 million valuation with like three people in an idea.

insights.claim: Gil's rule of thumb is that companies eventually trade at about 10x high-margin (70-80%) software revenue, so every $1 billion of valuation implies $50-100 million of fast-growing revenue; four-month-old companies at $1 billion only work if some become $100 billion-$1 trillion companies.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Use revenue-multiple back-solving to judge whether a private AI mark is plausible.
insights.quote: every billion dollars of market cap was eventually going to be $50 to $100 million of revenue growing rapidly

insights.claim: Gil says many AI startups are being priced as if they were Anthropic, with investors extrapolating large market size into fast adoption speed, which are two different things.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Discount startups whose valuations assume lab-like adoption curves in slower-moving markets.
insights.quote: I think a lot of um companies are being treated as if they're anthropic.

insights.claim: Gil argues most AI companies should consider exiting within the next 12-18 months because many are at the most valuable point they will ever be, and boards should formally discuss selling every six months given AI's clock speed.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Expect elevated AI M&A; for holders of private AI stakes, near-term liquidity may beat holding.
insights.quote: for many companies in AI, that's probably right around now.

insights.claim: Gil cites the dot-com precedent: roughly 2,000 internet companies IPO'd in the late 1990s and perhaps two dozen still exist; many that could have sold but did not went to zero.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Historical base rate argues most current AI winners-of-the-moment will not endure independently.
insights.quote: Many of the ones that could have sold but didn't went to zero.

insights.claim: Gil says companies from the 2020-2021 valuation upswing that turned down offers of hundreds of millions are now fire-saling or shutting down.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that refusing peak-cycle offers often destroys value; relevant for 2021-vintage portfolios.

insights.claim: Gil lists exit triggers: being paid years ahead of fundamentals, a large competitor entering and threatening growth (since buyers extrapolate growth rates), founder burnout or conflict, or a bigger-impact home at OpenAI, Anthropic or Google.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: A checklist for spotting AI startups likely to sell soon, e.g. those facing a lab entering their market.

insights.claim: Gil warns that the identity and growth of the acquirer matters: a $500 million offer in stock of a fast-growing buyer can beat a $1 billion offer from a flat one if the buyer 10xes, and leaving early forfeits unvested consideration.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: When evaluating AI M&A, value acquirer equity upside and retention vesting, not just headline price.

insights.claim: Gil holds that a handful of companies should never sell, citing Meta rejecting Yahoo's roughly $1 billion offer and Google refusing an early small offer.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: The sell-now thesis is a base rate, not universal; truly 10x-able companies should keep going.

themes.theme: Mega-cap ceilings and AI's share of GDP

insights.claim: Gil believes companies worth $10-20 trillion are plausible within a decade-plus, but a $100 trillion company (as Elon Musk tweeted about for SpaceX) would require at least $10 trillion of high-margin revenue against US GDP in the tens of trillions.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Sanity-check extreme market-cap targets against GDP share; the ceiling depends on AI expanding GDP rather than just capturing it.
insights.quote: I could definitely see companies being worth 10 trillion, 20 trillion, etc., within some decade plus time frame.

insights.claim: Gil's team roughly estimates that $100 billion of revenue each at OpenAI and Anthropic would be about half a percent of US GDP, and with cloud AI spend included AI models might be 0.5-1% of GDP, while much current GDP growth comes from data center buildouts.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: AI is still a small share of GDP but a large share of GDP growth via capex; data-center buildout is the macro channel to watch.
insights.quote: a lot of GDP growth right now is actually coming from data center buildouts

insights.claim: Gil pushes back on the idea that being a hyperscaler is the only durable trillion-dollar business, noting trillion-dollar companies now include Nvidia, Meta, Google, GLP-1 pharma makers, multiple semiconductor firms, and JP Morgan Chase near $800 billion-$1 trillion.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Trillion-dollar outcomes are spreading across sectors, broadening where mega-cap winners can emerge.

insights.claim: Gil attributes the proliferation of trillion-dollar companies to GDP growth, post-COVID inflation, and the internet acting as a global accelerant that lets products like Anthropic and OpenAI reach billions of people immediately.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Distribution at internet scale structurally raises the ceiling and speed of winners' growth.
insights.quote: the internet is basically an accelerant for growth for everything now

insights.claim: Gil says Elon Musk is the best founder of multiple hundreds of years.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Signals strong conviction in Musk-led companies such as SpaceX from a prominent investor.
insights.quote: I think that Elon Musk is the best founder of like multiple hundreds of years.

themes.theme: Bits vs atoms: where AI moves slower

insights.claim: Gil argues AI progresses fastest in closed-loop digital domains like code, where output can be tested and fed back to the model quickly, while biology and materials science need lab experiments and will move slower until they can be simulated in silico.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Discount AI-bio and AI-materials valuations that assume software-like timelines; watch for in-silico simulation breakthroughs.
insights.quote: those things are just definitionally going to take longer until you can move everything in silicone

insights.claim: Gil thinks biology may be nearing a cusp where enough generated data could let AI bootstrap rapidly into many new drugs and biopharma applications.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Data-generation platforms in bio could be the unlock; a potential inflection to monitor.

insights.claim: Gil expects personalized-medicine harnesses that let patients run their own data against AI models, citing GitLab founder Sid's self-directed cancer project, and says he knows stealth companies working in that area.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: AI-driven personalized-treatment tooling is an emerging venture category.

themes.theme: Gil's AI stack map: hits and misses

insights.claim: Gil's firm mapped AI four to five years ago as a stack: data centers and chips, foundation models (language, biology, physics, video), infrastructure, and B2B/B2C applications, investing in OpenAI, later Anthropic, incubating Brain Trust, and backing Harvey (legal), Cognition (code) and Decagon (customer support).
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: The application verticals that worked (legal, code, support) show where AI found early product-market fit.

insights.claim: Gil says expected AI category leaders in cyber security, sales enablement, financial tooling and accounting have not yet emerged, and he is unsure whether capabilities or something else is the blocker.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Open white space: these verticals may still produce large AI winners.
insights.quote: We thought there'd be like a giant um security company by now that was AI based.

insights.claim: Gil believes cyber will become a big AI category, possibly with multiple large companies, and just invested in a not-yet-public company he thinks could lead it.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: AI-native security is an area a top investor is actively backing now.

insights.claim: Gil backs AI-driven roll-ups that buy services businesses and transform them with AI, citing Long Lake, which had bought 30-40 companies and recently took a business travel company private, and Ithaca, which just took another company private.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: AI-enabled services take-privates are an active strategy; watch services-heavy public small caps as targets.

insights.claim: Gil says one of his biggest mistakes was assuming every market is a monopoly; many are oligopolies (payments has a dozen giants, pharma usually has three or four providers of a drug type), and AI labs stay an oligopoly while compute constraints prevent anyone from pulling far ahead.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Underwrite multiple winners per AI market; compute scarcity structurally sustains several labs.
insights.quote: one of the biggest mistakes I ever made was assuming that everything's a monopoly

insights.claim: Gil says 80-90% of the code at the model companies is now generated by their own AI, with AI increasingly proposing research experiments, which is the path to recursive self-improvement where each model builds the next.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Accelerating RSI implies faster model cadence and capability jumps, reinforcing lab leadership and compute demand.
insights.quote: it's shifting to like 80 90% of the code base is now being generated by AI

insights.claim: Gil notes most of a frontier lab's core research cost is now compute rather than people, and a few hundred researchers generate most of the best ideas, so allocating compute to them and to AI researchers is extremely valuable.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Lab economics are compute-bound; supports sustained compute demand and extreme pay for top researchers.
insights.quote: most of your cost now is compute it's not people

insights.claim: Gil says the most cutting-edge AI, such as agentic swarms collaborating on software and research, is now concentrated inside a very small number of labs rather than accessible to everyone as early GPT APIs were.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Edge comes from proximity to lab insiders; outsiders see capabilities with a lag.

themes.theme: Founder quality, defense and other sector views

insights.claim: Gil says founder quality spiked in 2021-2022 after the ZIRP era of 'larping' founders, but the AI gold rush is now bringing opportunistic fake founders back, producing a mixed pool.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Diligence on founder quality matters more now; not every hot AI team is the 2022-vintage caliber.
insights.quote: Now we're in a little bit of a mixed era where because it looks like AI is a way to make a quick buck. We have more of the larpers again.

insights.claim: Gil's founder signals: competitive and driven, strong at selling, concise, technical root-cause thinkers, great product taste (Cursor, Cognition, Perplexity), strong bias to ship, and good taste in people; showing something built in a week beats articulate storytelling.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: A reusable founder-screening rubric from an investor with strong AI hit rate.
insights.quote: if somebody shows up with something built, even if it was just in a week, it's usually a better sign than somebody who's just talking about it very articulately

insights.claim: Gil says defense has shifted from a quasi-vice category to mainstream; when he funded Anduril about a decade ago it was very unpopular, though some large institutions still distinguish defensive from offensive.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Institutional acceptance of defense tech widens the capital base for the sector.

insights.claim: Gil says the rare earth mineral market is neither rare nor large and is largely price-manipulated by Chinese government intervention; his firm also invests in supply-chain repatriation, redundancy, power generation and grid upgrades for data centers.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Treat rare-earth hype with caution; grid and power for data centers is where he is deploying.

insights.claim: Gil sees no fundamental difference between prediction markets and gambling, citing Polymarket and Kalshi as having moved vice-like betting into new forms.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Regulatory treatment of prediction markets may converge with gambling, a key risk for the category.
insights.quote: I mean what's the difference between a prediction market and gambling? >> I don't think there is.

insights.claim: Gil's literature review, cross-checked with Claude and ChatGPT, found no solid evidence that microplastics harm humans (the key inflammation assay was flawed), though phthalates look concerning in mouse models; he sees anti-plastic sentiment as possibly like nuclear's anti-progress stigma.
insights.speaker: Elad Gil
insights.so_what: Weakens the scientific case behind anti-plastic regulation; relevant to packaging and chemicals exposure.
